analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes to report staffing publicly and face unannounced checks when understaffing harms residents.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it died in committee four weeks after introduction, with no cosponsors, when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nursing homes paid by Medicare and Medicaid to report their nurse staffing hours and wages to the government, with the results published on the federal 'Nursing Home Compare' website so families could compare facilities before choosing one [S3]. When inspectors found a quality problem that hurt a resident and traced it to too few nurses, the home would have had to fix it within 30 days and then face surprise follow-up inspections to verify it [S3]. It was introduced on December 7, 2000, referred to the Ways and Means and Commerce Committees, sent to two health subcommittees, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families. Families would have seen each facility's actual staffing hours and wages on a public website before choosing a home [S3]. Residents in facilities where understaffing contributed to real harm would have gotten mandatory corrections within 30 days and unannounced follow-up inspections for at least two years [S3]. Nurses and aides could also gain, since facilities would have to document how many staff hours residents actually receive.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires every Medicare- and Medicaid-certified nursing facility to report total nurse staffing hours per shift, broken down by nurses' aides, practical nurses, and registered nurses, plus average wage rates for each class of staff.
Directs HHS to publish that facility-specific staffing data on the 'Nursing Home Compare' Internet site and update it periodically, letting families compare facilities before placement.

Requires inspectors to assess whether inadequate nurse staffing contributed to any quality deficiency that caused a resident actual harm or posed an immediate safety risk, and to conduct two unannounced follow-up surveys if it did — with civil fines for anyone who leaks the inspection date to the facility.
Requires a facility found deficient due to understaffing to specify in its correction plan exactly how many additional nurses of each type it must hire, and to implement the plan within 30 days.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing facilities, which would face new data-reporting paperwork, unannounced follow-up inspections when understaffing is linked to harm, and the underlying cost of hiring enough nurses to meet the staffing adequacy review. Consumers indirectly, to the extent facilities raise prices to cover added staffing or compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds reporting paperwork on facilities but sets no specific staffing ratio and defines 'adequate' staffing only through an annual HHS review, so enforcement would depend heavily on how regulators interpreted the data.
Requiring staffing and wage data collection per shift and resident classification imposes administrative costs on facilities, costs that small or rural operators would bear alongside large chains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — verifiable, public staffing information and surprise re-inspections when understaffing causes harm — is targeted and modest in cost, mostly paperwork plus staffing where care was already found deficient. The main honest objection is that transparency alone does not force a staffing level; but requiring a correction plan to specify the exact number of additional nurses within 30 days pushes it beyond pure disclosure.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with no cosponsors on December 7, 2000, it was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees and sat there until the 106th Congress ended four weeks later, never reaching a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on December 7, 2000, during the final weeks of the 106th Congress.

The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Commerce Committee on the day of introduction, then sent to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health on December 11 and the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment on December 13.
No further action was taken, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The nursing facility industry is better off: it avoided the staffing-data reporting, unannounced follow-up inspections, and 30-day correction requirements the bill would have imposed. Nursing home residents and families did not get the staffing transparency it promised — though HHS later moved to publish staffing data on its own, separate from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor on December 7, 2000.

sides.party_line_note: No party bloc ever took a position: the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died in committee without a hearing or vote.

industries.note: Facilities would have had to report staffing hours and wages publicly, submit to unannounced re-inspections whenever understaffing contributed to resident harm, and hire additional nurses within 30 days of a deficiency finding. Understaffing is a direct labor-cost saving for facilities, so the bill's requirement to publish staffing data and fix deficiencies squarely works against the industry's operating margin — and in favor of residents' care.
